sentences.text: The head of Psarolepis was constructed from several thick dermal plates covered in deep pock-marks and large pores.
These pock-marked head plates contained a layer of porcelain-like material known as cosmine.
Psarolepis had a strangely humped snout with nostrils positioned above the eyes, which were located just above the upper jaw.
The premaxilla and dentary bones featured large inner teeth alongside an irregular array of tiny outer teeth.
Psarolepis possessed a unique feature called 'parasymphysical tooth whorls,' where teeth extended upward at the front of the lower jaw.
The fin spines found in Psarolepis are characteristic of primitive jawed fishes, absent in the most primitive sharks, but common in more derived forms.
Fossils of Psarolepis were primarily found in South China and the genus was described by paleontologist Xiaobo Yu in 1998.
Most Psarolepis fossils were discovered at the Yulongsi, Xishancun, and Xitun Formations, located about 10 km northwest of Qujing, Yunnan, China.
Remains of Psarolepis were collected in 1981 and 1984 by paleontologist Min Zhu and colleagues and dated to the Early Devonian and Late Silurian periods.
When first described in 1998, Psarolepis was classified as a sarcopterygian (lobe-finned fish) due to skull and jaw similarities to primitive lungfishes.
In 2001, researchers Zhu and Schultze provided evidence suggesting Psarolepis was likely a basal bony fish.
The Paleobiology Database lists the parent group of Psarolepis as Sarcopterygii.
Psarolepis is classified within the class Osteichthyes.
Psarolepis was an extinct genus of bony fish that lived between 418 and 397 million years ago during the Pridoli and Lochkovian stages.
The time range for Psarolepis is recorded as 422.7 to 413.02 million years ago, spanning the Pridoli to Lochkovian periods.
